title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a deep dive into what many consider Dickens's strangest, richest, most audacious novel.
Our Mutual Friend was his last completed novel, published in 1864 and 1865, and it is a book obsessed with money, with identity, with the dead rising and the living pretending to be dead.
At its centre is a fortune built on dust mounds — heaps of Victorian refuse that somehow become the engine of an entire social world.
I'm joined today by three people who love this novel deeply and argue about it passionately.
Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing professor who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — always looking for what makes it move.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels for audio than almost anyone alive, and he hears Dickens's prose the way a musician hears a score — for rhythm, timing, and the comic spark.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Our Mutual Friend as a teenager and has been returning to it ever since — she brings the reader's eye, and the reader's heart.
Let's begin with the great animating themes of this novel — money, dust, and the question of whether goodness can survive in a world built on both.
What strikes me first, every time, is how ruthlessly Dickens ties virtue to the social machinery he most despises.
The Boffins — Nicodemus and Henrietta — are, by every surface measure, ignorant and unpolished people.
They have come up through the dust trade, through decades of being wrung for labour and paid as little as possible.
And yet Dickens makes this absolutely radical claim about them — that even the hardened, sordid nature of old Harmon could not quite extinguish what he saw in them.
He builds to it in the most extraordinary way.
"For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never."
Five words at the end — but Good, never — and the whole chapter swings on them like a door.
That is Dickens the moralist operating at the height of his compression.
You know what I love about that line — and I have read it aloud more times than I can count — is that it absolutely refuses to be subtle.
Dickens is not whispering a theme at you.
He is standing on a chair and announcing it to the room.
And when you perform that passage, you feel how he has earned it — all those clauses about weaknesses, vanities, the sordid nature of old Harmon — they are the winding of a spring.
And then the spring releases: but Good, never.
What moves me is the generosity of it.
Dickens is defending people who cannot defend themselves in the world of the novel — people who would be patronised or dismissed by almost every other character in it.
The line about ten thousand weaknesses and absurdities — he does not pretend the Boffins are perfect.
He says, yes, they are flawed, and yes, the goodness is still real, and yes, it outlasts the evil that tried to use them.
That is a rather beautiful argument to make through characters who are essentially comic grotesques.
And of course the Boffins' goodness is tested in the most extreme way later in the novel — when John Harmon, restored to his true identity, finally confronts the parasite Silas Wegg.
Oliver, you've performed that scene — what's happening there?
It is one of the great denunciation scenes in Dickens — and Dickens knew how to write a denunciation.
Harmon has been living in disguise as John Rokesmith, watching everything, knowing everything, and now the mask comes off entirely.
And what he says about the Boffins — it is practically a speech of thanks at a memorial service.
He says — and I love the parenthesis here, it is so characteristic — he says:
"I owe everything I possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness, goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin."
There are no words to satisfy me — in the middle of a furious speech, through clenched teeth, Harmon stops to confess that language is not enough.
That is not the move of a hack novelist.
And it connects directly back to what we were just reading — the eternal law, Good never dying.
The Boffins' goodness is not abstract — it has practical consequences across the whole arc of the plot.
Harmon inherits his fortune not through his father's intention — his father tried to use that fortune as a weapon — but through the Boffins' voluntary generosity.
Good outlasts the doer of evil.
The novel enacts exactly what that sentence promises.
I want to linger on the identity question for a moment, because it is so central to everything.
Harmon spends most of this novel as someone else — as Rokesmith, watching his own inheritance from the outside.
And Dickens actually steps forward in the novel's postscript — breaks the fictional frame entirely — to address readers who had guessed too quickly.
He is not defensive about it — he is rather magnificent, actually.
He writes — and this is Dickens speaking directly to us across the page:

"I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he."
I love the sheer nerve of it — he is telling readers, I knew you thought you were cleverer than me, and I was counting on it.
It is the most gentlemanly possible way of saying — you were wrong, and I planned it that way.
And he wraps it in this rather beautiful plea for patience with the artist — that the audience might concede him a little patience in his vocation.
Which is either deeply humble or extremely confident, and I suspect it is both at once.
Money built on dust, goodness outlasting evil, a man hiding inside his own story — these are the currents that run through everything we'll discuss today.
Coming up: we turn to the river, and to the two men who fish it for very different prizes.

segments.title: Bella's Education in Love and Loss

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show where we take Dickens's last completed novel apart — carefully, lovingly — to see how it works.
Today we're deep inside Bella Wilfer's story — the question of what she is, what she might become, and whether the man who loves her has any right to put her to the test.
With me are three readers I trust completely with these pages.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who cares about how fiction is made — the architecture, the sentences, the single image that carries a chapter's weight.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels on audio than almost anyone alive, and he hears Dickens the way a conductor hears a score — rhythm, timing, comedy, grief.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has never quite left it — she reads for pleasure, for feeling, and for the verbal music Dickens hides in plain sight.
Let's begin with money — Dickens's great curse word in this novel — and with a child who has nothing.
There's a passage early in this stretch of the novel that I find almost unbearable to read — and I mean that as the highest praise.
Lizzie Hexam is explaining the situation of this poor sick child to her brother Charley.
The father is a drunk, the mother is dead, and Dickens gives us the whole catastrophe in one devastating sentence.
Lizzie says — and this is Dickens at his most compressed —
'This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle — if she ever had one, Charley.'
'If she ever had one.' Four words. That parenthesis is everything.
It reaches all the way back past poverty into a kind of negation of childhood itself.
That parenthesis is doing something genuinely strange, technically speaking.
It's not a digression — it's a retraction.
Dickens gives you the image of a cradle, then immediately withdraws even that comfort.
And it's Lizzie who says it — not the narrator, not Dickens editorializing from on high.
It comes out of someone who grew up on the river, who knows what deprivation actually looks like.
That makes it far more devastating than any authorial lament could be.
And then notice what the passage does next — it doesn't dwell.
Dickens moves straight on. The restraint is the art.
As someone who has spoken that line aloud more than once, I can tell you that the hardest part is not rushing it.
Performers always want to do something with 'if she ever had one.' Give it a tremor. A catch in the voice.
But the line works precisely because Lizzie says it simply, without self-pity. She's just stating a fact she's lived alongside.
What kills me is the address to Charley at the end. That final word — 'Charley.'
It's a reminder: you came from this too. You are not a visitor to this world. You are of it.
And it's against that world — that world of waste and degradation — that John Harmon's story runs.
Because we get, in these chapters, his extraordinary interior confession — almost a legal deposition he gives to himself.
Eleanor, what is Dickens doing structurally with that soliloquy?
It's one of the most audacious pieces of narrative engineering in the whole novel.
Harmon essentially puts himself on trial — and he's simultaneously the accused, the prosecutor, and the judge.
What clinches that effect is the punctuation. The self-corrections. 'Is that so? That is exactly so.'
And listen to how the passage begins — Harmon cataloguing his own dread as he returned to England.
'I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife.'
That triple repetition — shrinking, shrinking, mistrustful — it's almost liturgical.
Dickens is giving us a man whose conscience moves in ritual rhythms because he has nowhere else to put the guilt.
The rhythm of it is what gets me when I read it aloud.
There's something almost desperate in all that shrinking. He's recoiling from his own inheritance.
And yet he came back. That's what the passage makes you feel.
The duty and the dread are pulling in opposite directions — and he came back anyway.
What I find harder to defend is what he decides to do with that return.
Ah — now we get to the scheme. And it is a scheme, let's be honest about that.
He and this man Radfoot — a stranger on a ship, someone whose honesty he has absolutely no way of verifying — cook up a plot to spy on Bella Wilfer.
And Dickens gives it to us with a kind of breezy detail that I think is deliberate.
The plot was, as Harmon tells it, to dress as common sailors —
'the plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses, and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way.'
'Throwing ourselves in her neighbourhood.' It sounds almost comic, doesn't it? Almost like farce.
But Dickens lets the absurdity stand next to the genuine moral question — which is: what gives him the right?
Exactly — and Dickens faces that question directly in the next chapter.
There's that remarkable passage where Harmon — now as Rokesmith — goes over the whole thing again, trying to justify it to himself.
And Dickens is scrupulously honest about the trap Rokesmith has set for himself.
The deception began, Dickens tells us —

'it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was honestly meant well towards her.'
'Honestly meant well.' That phrase carries an enormous amount of water.
Because good intentions and good actions are not the same thing — and this novel knows that better than almost any other.
That passage is a masterclass in what I'd call moral accounting — Dickens holding every item in the ledger up to the light.
Notice how the chapter goes over the same ground twice: once in Harmon's own voice, then in the narrator's.
The narrator's version is the one that really turns the screw —

'When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless.'
'Never yet for good within his knowledge then.' That qualifier — 'within his knowledge then' — is Dickens being morally precise.
He's not saying the money was never good — he's saying Rokesmith had never seen it be good. That's a crucial distinction.
The novel is slowly building a case that education — real moral education — comes from experience, not inheritance.
And then there's Mr Boffin — who provides, bless him, the comic relief that this section desperately needs.
The passage where Boffin goes off about charity patrons is pure Dickensian satirical delight.
He's ranting, and you have to hear the list to believe it —

'Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!'
The escalation of that list — it just keeps going, each category more absurd than the last — is Dickens at his most musically comic.
And then Boffin lands the verdict: 'If it ain't stark staring impudence, what do you call it?' Perfect.
What I love is that Boffin's rant isn't just comedy — it's his moral education of Bella working by indirection.
He's showing her what money looks like when it metastasises into status — into these absurd hierarchies of patronage.
Deceased Patrons. Ex-Vice-Patronesses. It's a graveyard of self-congratulation.
And Bella is watching. She's learning what wealth at its most grotesque looks like — from the inside.
So we have the poor child with no cradle, the man who built a deception out of distrust, and the grotesque comedy of inherited wealth performing its own generosity.
All of it converging on one question: what does Bella become?
And perhaps a harder question still — has John Harmon earned the right to have helped shape the answer?
We'll sit with that — and with John Harmon's extraordinary moment of self-reckoning — after the break.

segments.title: The Wit and Folly of Fleet Street

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart to see how it works — and why it still works so brilliantly.
I'm your host, and today we're deep in the comic engine room of the book — the wit, the folly, the magnificent human absurdity.
With me today are three people whose company I find entirely equal to the occasion.
Dr Eleanor Hartley teaches creative writing and thinks about how great novelists build their effects — the architecture beneath the surface.
Oliver Trevelyan has read more Dickens aloud than perhaps any person alive, and hears rhythms and comic timing that the rest of us might miss on the page.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has loved this novel since her teens and reads it with the devotion it deserves.
Oliver, I want to start with you — because Dickens introduces Twemlow in a way that is, on its face, completely deranged.
He compares a human being to a dining table — and somehow makes it feel entirely natural.
It is deranged — gloriously, methodically, cold-bloodedly deranged.
What I love is that Dickens commits entirely to the conceit and never winks at you.
He introduces Twemlow as, and I'm quoting directly here,
'an innocent piece of dinner-furniture that went upon easy castors and was kept over a livery stable-yard in Duke Street, Saint James's, when not in use.'
Dinner-furniture. On castors. Kept over a stable-yard.
This is not metaphor as decoration — this is metaphor as social diagnosis.
And then comes the line that makes me laugh every single time I read it aloud.
'Being first cousin to Lord Snigsworth, he was in frequent requisition, and at many houses might be said to represent the dining-table in its normal state.'
'The dining-table in its normal state.' That phrase alone earns the whole passage.
What strikes me structurally is how the metaphor then does actual work — it isn't just a joke.
Dickens extends it — Mr and Mrs Veneering start with Twemlow and then 'put leaves in him.'
And crucially: the more Twemlow is pulled out, the further he finds himself from the centre.
That's the social geometry of the whole novel spelled out in a furniture analogy.
The more useful you are to the Veneerings, the more marginal you become.
It's a beautiful piece of compression — a whole satirical argument folded into a domestic image.
I always feel slightly sorry for Twemlow.
The comedy is merciless, but there's something quietly melancholy underneath it.
He's genuinely confused by the Veneerings — there's that lovely phrase, 'a source of blind confusion.'
He doesn't understand them, and they don't see him.
They see a table — expandable, retractable, storable over a stable-yard when not required.
That's what Dickens is doing with laughter in this novel — using it as a way to show us something genuinely sad about how these people live.
Caroline is absolutely right, and it's why the comedy lands so hard — it has bones.
Now — can we please talk about Sloppy? Because Sloppy in his black suit is one of the great comic set-pieces in the whole book.
There's been a valiant attempt to dress him properly — the tailor has been given personal directions to conceal the buttons.
But listen to what happens:
'he now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators.'
A perfect Argus. One hundred eyes of bright metal.
Sloppy's body has simply defeated tailoring science — and Dickens makes that sound like a force of nature, unstoppable and magnificent.
It keeps going: the hat has 'a black bunch, from which the imagination shrunk discomfited and the reason revolted.'
The imagination shrunk discomfited. I would have that framed.
What Dickens is doing technically there is giving inanimate things — the buttons, the hatband, the sleeves — a kind of aggressive agency.
The clothes are acting. Sloppy is almost passive — he 'stands confessed,' as the passage ends.
That phrase — 'Sloppy stood confessed' — has a mock-judicial weight to it, as if the suit has prosecuted him and won.
The comedy is coming from syntax as much as from imagery.
The accumulation — 'shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling' — is Dickens deliberately overdoing it, piling on until you have to laugh.
And yet — and I feel this strongly — Sloppy himself is entirely loveable.
The comedy is never at his expense in a cruel way.
Dickens is laughing with him — there's a warmth to every one of those gleaming buttons.
Which is what makes Sloppy's moment of triumph later so joyful — and Oliver, I believe you have strong feelings about that scene.
Strong feelings is putting it mildly.
Sloppy's reappearance — in the scene where Wegg finally gets what's coming to him — is one of the most satisfying comic coups Dickens ever pulled off.
The staging is pure theatre. Someone has crept in quietly through the folding-doors.
'Turning his head, Wegg beheld his persecutor, the ever-wakeful dustman, accoutred with fantail hat and velveteen smalls complete.'
And then — the reveal.
'Who, untying his tied-up broken head, revealed a head that was whole, and a face that was Sloppy's.'
'A face that was Sloppy's.' Five words. The whole audience — reading audience or listening audience — just erupts.
Dickens has been hiding Sloppy in plain sight, and the costume — that absurd dustman's outfit — circles back from the comedy of the suit to the comedy of the disguise.
There's a structural rhyme there that I find genuinely thrilling.
Sloppy's clothing was the joke — unable to be contained, overflowing with buttons and bagged knees.
Now the costume is weaponised — it becomes the instrument of justice.
Dickens is recycling his comic energy, turning it toward a moral purpose.
And speaking of things being weaponised — we should discuss Wegg's scheme against Boffin, because that passage is a masterclass in comic villainy.
Wegg lays out this elaborate plan with tremendous self-importance — he keeps calling Venus his 'comrade, brother, and partner.'
And the heart of the scheme is one magnificent word — which he delivers, I imagine, with tremendous theatrical weight:
'he considered it plain that such price was stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, Halves!'
And then he goes on to suggest it might more properly be two-thirds.
Or three-fourths.
He's 'ever open to correction.' The man is a comic monument.
What I find darkly funny is the language Wegg uses for Boffin — 'the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour.'
It has the grandeur of a manifesto — Wegg genuinely believes in his own rhetoric.
And then that final phrase — Boffin is to be kept in 'a state of abject moral bondage and slavery.'
'abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his possessions.'
The self-aggrandising pomposity of it is wonderful — and entirely self-defeating, as we know.
The comic register and the moral register are perfectly aligned here.
Before we leave the comic high points entirely — can we take a moment for Rokesmith's declaration to Bella?
Because Dickens writes it with this tone of delighted mock-astonishment — as if he himself can barely believe he's allowed to write something this good.
Rokesmith comes rushing in and he cries —
'My dear, dear girl; my gallant, generous, disinterested, courageous, noble girl!'
And then Dickens adds, with that parenthetical wink of his — 'which one might have thought astonishment enough for one dose' —
and Bella 'lifted it up and laid it on his breast, as if that were her head's chosen and lasting resting-place.'
The comedy and the tenderness are completely inseparable — and that's Dickens at his most characteristic.
That phrase — 'her head's chosen and lasting resting-place' — is doing everything.
It's romantic, yes — but 'chosen' carries such moral weight in a novel that has been asking what we choose and why we choose it.
And 'lasting' insists on permanence — it's not the comedy of the moment but a promise.
Dickens gets away with sentimentality when the words can bear that much thinking about.
What's so striking in everything we've discussed today is how the comedy in this novel is never merely decorative — it's load-bearing.
From Twemlow on his castors to Sloppy's hundred gleaming buttons to Wegg's magnificent 'Halves!' — the laughs carry the meaning.
My thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Oliver Trevelyan, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation I could happily have continued for another hour.
We'll be back with more from Our Mutual Friend very soon.
Welcome to this segment of Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, where we turn our close attention to the moral and emotional world surrounding the Boffins.
Nicodemus Boffin — the Golden Dustman — is one of Dickens's most carefully constructed figures: a man whose goodness is tested, observed, and ultimately ratified by the novel itself.
Today we're looking at several passages that together build a kind of moral portrait: a man of genuine virtue, surrounded by every variety of human cupidity.
Eleanor Hartley is here — novelist, craft reader, and someone who never lets Dickens off the hook for structural choices she finds irresistible.
Oliver Trevelyan joins us — the man who has performed more Dickens than anyone alive, and who hears these passages the way a conductor hears a score.
And Caroline Woodcourt is with us — a critic and lifelong reader who came to this novel as a teenager and has never quite left it.
Eleanor, I want to start with you — with that extraordinary passage in which Boffin recalls the last time he and Mrs Boffin saw young John Harmon.
What is Dickens doing architecturally, in that scene?
What strikes me first is the way Dickens chooses to give this memory to Boffin in his own voice — not filtered through the omniscient narrator.
Boffin speaks in the rhythms of a man without formal education — the repeated constructions, the slight grammatical looseness — and yet what comes through is absolute moral clarity.
The detail that undoes me — the structural detail — is the doubling of 'scanty.'
Listen to how Dickens places it, because the syntax here is doing enormous work.
"There was his little scanty travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in the shivering wind."
The anaphora — 'There was... there was' — is a lament in miniature.
And 'scanty' applied first to clothes, then to the box — it tells us everything about how this child has been deprived.
Not just materially deprived — emotionally diminished, sent out into the world with almost nothing.
Eleanor, yes — and what I notice as a performer is that this whole passage is written to be spoken aloud by someone exactly like Boffin.
It has the rhythm of a man finding the words as he speaks them — feeling his way through a painful memory.
And then it arrives at Mrs Boffin's cry, which Dickens writes as if she's still in the room saying it.
"I'd give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!"
The repetition of 'wide' — 'the wide wide world' — is a child's phrase, a nursery phrase.
And 'I would' thrust in the middle — that's not elegance, that's desperation, that's a real person speaking.
Dickens knew that the truest emotion arrives in fractured syntax.
What I can't let go of is the moment at the end of that memory — where Mrs Boffin and Boffin decide never to wish for a child of their own.
Because they've seen what happens to children who are loved and then lost.
The passage that haunts me is Mrs Boffin waking in the night.

"Of a night, when it was very cold, or when the wind roared, or the rain dripped heavy, she would wake sobbing, and call out in a fluster, 'Don't you see the poor child's face? O shelter the poor child!'"
That cry — 'O shelter the poor child' — it breaks open the whole novel's concern with what wealth should be for.
The Boffins receive a fortune, and behind them is this woman who has been calling out in her sleep to protect a child who was already gone.
And that is the context in which old John Harmon names them in his will.
Dickens is quite explicit about why — and it's one of the most devastating sentences he writes about the powerlessness of money.
The narrator tells us that the old miser had perceived something he could never forgive and never ignore.
"He had perceived the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt."
The whole structure of that sentence turns on 'if he had addressed himself to the attempt' — which implies he almost did.
He considered trying to corrupt them. He knew he would fail. And that knowledge is what saves them — and possibly him.
There's something almost Shakespearean in that construction — the villain who acknowledges virtue precisely by recognising he cannot purchase it.
And Dickens gives us that parenthetical sting — 'he mistrusted all who bore any resemblance to himself.'
Which means the only people he could trust were people utterly unlike him.
The Boffins qualify for his trust precisely because they don't share his values at all.
And then the fortune arrives — and with it, an absolute deluge.
The passages about the begging letters are among the funniest Dickens ever wrote, and also among the most pointed.
He itemises every variety of fraud with a kind of gleeful precision.
My favourite is the ducal letter — the 'large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.'
"Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet."
Four adjectives before the noun — and every one of them indicting the sender.
'Large' — it's important. 'Fat' — it's self-satisfied. 'Private' — it's conspiratorial. 'Double' — it costs more to post.
The postscript about the three-guinea fee is a masterclass in comic timing.
Dickens puts it in parentheses: 'thoughtful in the postscript' — deadpan, devastating.
And then immediately undercuts the personal warmth of it — 'only lithographed by the hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address.'
But then the individual beggars arrive — and that's where Dickens does something even more extraordinary.
He catalogues them in taxonomic categories — the inspired beggars, the nobly independent beggars, the beggars of punctual business-habits.
It reads like a grotesque field guide to human desperation and human dishonesty, often in the same person.
And then this — on the documentation they all enclose.
"They call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf."
That simile is vicious and completely perfect.
And all of this — the begging letters, the ducal charity rackets, the inspired beggars with their angelic visitations — it's structural.
Dickens is building a world in which everyone who encounters money is corroded by it — except the Boffins.
And that moral contrast is confirmed, in a darkly comic way, by the second will — the one Wegg discovers.
Old Harmon writes Boffin down for almost nothing — 'the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him' — as though virtue deserves only modest reward.

"Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown."
'Quite enough for him' — there's contempt in those words, but also, perhaps, a kind of grudging accuracy.
For Boffin, it probably would have been enough.
That detail — 'he has never made friends' — lands differently once you've read the Boffin memory.
Because we know that someone tried to be a friend to John Harmon's son.
Mrs Boffin warmed his cheeks by the fire and called out for him in her sleep for years.
The old man left the Boffins a fortune without ever understanding what they were actually offering him — and what he refused.
We've moved from a child's tears by a fireplace to a miser's last will — and what connects them is the question of what wealth is for, and who deserves it.
In our next segment, we turn to another dimension of Our Mutual Friend: the river, and the dark labour of those who live by it.
Eleanor, Oliver, Caroline — thank you.

segments.title: Secrets and Schemes: Plot's Machinery Exposed

utterances.text: Welcome to this segment of Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, where we pull back the curtain on the novel's plotting — its secrets, its schemes, its machinery of revelation and comic justice.
Our Mutual Friend is one of the most elaborately plotted novels in English fiction — identities concealed, fortunes disputed, alliances struck and broken.
And yet Dickens never lets the machinery become cold — he keeps it warm with character, and wickedly funny at the hinges.
With us today: Eleanor Hartley, novelist and creative writing teacher, who reads for the architecture behind the effects.
Oliver Trevelyan, actor and the voice behind more Dickens audiobooks than anyone should reasonably attempt, who hears the prose before he reads it.
And Caroline Woodcourt, book critic and devoted re-reader of this novel, who brings the perspective of someone who has lived with these characters across many years.
Let's begin with the river — and a moment of violent severance that opens the novel's first real confrontation.
Gaffer Hexam is a man who lives by the river and speaks in its rhythms — short, hard, without ceremony.
He is cutting off his former partner in their grim trade of fishing corpses from the Thames, and he does it with the efficiency of someone who has cut a line before.
What Dickens gives us is this extraordinary compressed dismissal — listen to the final two commands.
"Let go. Cast off!"
Two imperatives. Two syllables each. An entire relationship ended in four words.
On the page it's stark. Read aloud, it lands like a blade.
That compression is so telling — because Gaffer's whole characterisation runs on suppression rather than expression.
Dickens is usually a maximalist, but for Gaffer he applies a kind of brutal economy — the voice matches the man.
What I find structurally interesting is what precedes those two commands — the whole speech is about moral self-distinction.
Gaffer draws a line between himself and the boatman's pocket-picking — as if there is a hierarchy of crimes among those who scavenge the dead.
He is, in his own mind, the honest man of the river. The novel is going to make him pay dearly for that self-image.
And Lizzie is there, watching all of this.
That's what I find so quietly devastating about the opening scenes — Lizzie's education is this: watching her father sever ties, make threats, declare his own code.
She absorbs all of it. She has no choice. The river is her inheritance long before any Harmon money enters the picture.
And that inheritance is contested from the very first page — which brings us to the Harmon fortune, and the Boffins.
Because what is so remarkable about Mr and Mrs Boffin is that they arrive as beneficiaries — and immediately try to give the benefit away.
Oliver, you've been looking at the scene where Mr Boffin recounts the history of old Harmon's cruelty to young John — let's go there.
Mr Boffin is one of Dickens's great gifts to anyone who performs this novel — he speaks in a dialect that is completely his own.
Warm, slightly fractured grammar, tremendous moral seriousness wearing the costume of a cheerful muddle.
He is telling Mortimer Lightwood about the cruelties of old Harmon — and then he produces this extraordinary image.

"I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet — she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head — and send it spinning across the yard."
And it only gets better — because he continues: "and received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her."
"Which dropped her." The repetition is everything. Boffin cannot quite believe it even now.
The parenthetical about the bonnet is extraordinary craft — it looks like a digression but it's doing three things at once.
It fixes Mrs Boffin in our minds as a vivid physical presence — a woman with a black straw bonnet perched for convenience, not vanity.
It makes the violence that follows more visceral because we can see the specific object spinning.
And it is simultaneously comic and horrible — which is exactly the tonal register Dickens needs to establish the Boffins as people of genuine suffering and genuine warmth.
What moves me is that Boffin is recounting all of this as context — almost as evidence — for why he and Mrs Boffin care so deeply about young John Harmon's memory.
They took the blows. Literally, in Mrs Boffin's case. And they kept going back.
That is what makes Mrs Boffin's idea — when she proposes finding an orphan child — feel earned rather than sentimental.
And that proposal — Mrs Boffin's plan to adopt an orphan boy and name him John Harmon — is one of the novel's most unexpectedly tender moments.
Caroline, you've been sitting with that passage — what does it do to the novel's architecture of identity?
There is something almost ghostly about the idea — and Dickens knows it.
Mrs Boffin is proposing to bring a living child into the space vacated by a dead one — and to give him the dead child's name.
The novel is, of course, simultaneously concealing from us that John Harmon is not dead at all — he is moving through its pages in disguise.
So Mrs Boffin's speech carries a weight she cannot know it carries.

Her exact words are: "Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him."
That cadence — the listing of small, accumulating kindnesses — is so characteristic of her.
And then she adds: "Say it's only a whim" — which is the most Mrs Boffin sentence in the entire novel.
The double irony is quite dizzying when you stop to think about it.
Mrs Boffin wants to name a substitute for John Harmon — while the real John Harmon is operating nearby under a substitute name.
Identity in this novel is never stable — it is always a kind of performance, a costume, a name chosen or imposed.
And Dickens plants this resonance in what sounds like a sentimental domestic conversation — that is the structural genius of it.
And of course the rooftop scene with Lizzie and Jenny Wren turns this theme of refuge and reinvention into something almost pastoral — extraordinary given that they're surrounded by chimneys.
Riah has made them a little world up there — a carpet, some fruit, books, a creeper growing over a blackened chimney-stack.

Dickens describes it with such care: "Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren — for whom, perhaps with some old instinct of his race, the gentle Jew had spread a carpet — they both pored over one book; both with attentive faces."
"Jenny with the sharper; Lizzie with the more perplexed." Two words each. Two entire characters.
And then there are those chimneys — "twirling their cowls and fluttering their smoke" — described as dowager ladies bridling and fanning themselves.
It's comic, but it's also a kind of benediction — even the industrial landscape is giving these two women an amused nod of approval.
What I love is that Fledgeby stumbles into this scene not knowing what he's seeing.
He is a creature of schemes and small greed — and here are two women reading, on a rooftop, surrounded by their little garden of strings and beads.
It is one of the most quietly radical images in the novel — two women of no social consequence, quietly making a life above the city's noise.
And if the rooftop garden represents the novel at its most lyrical and quietly hopeful, what comes next might be its most savagely comic set-piece.
Oliver — Silas Wegg and his exit from the novel.
Silas Wegg is a magnificent, absolutely irredeemable villain — and he deserves every syllable of what Dickens does to him.
The disposal is carried out by Sloppy — the great shambling innocent of the novel — who treats Wegg precisely like the sack of flour or coals he resembles.
The instructions were to deposit him in the road. But a scavenger's cart happened to be waiting, and Dickens cannot resist — nor can Sloppy.
Here is the sentence — and it is a masterpiece of deadpan comic prose:

"Mr Sloppy's instructions had been to deposit his burden in the road; but, a scavenger's cart happening to stand unattended at the corner, with its little ladder planted against the wheel, Mr S. found it impossible to resist the temptation of shooting Mr Silas Wegg into the cart's contents."
"A somewhat difficult feat, achieved with great dexterity, and with a prodigious splash."
"A prodigious splash." Three words. The whole squalid career of Silas Wegg, summarised.
That final sentence has a syntactic formality — "A somewhat difficult feat, achieved with great dexterity" — that is itself the joke.
It sounds like a report. A citation for gallantry. And the subject is a scheming fraudster being thrown into a rubbish cart.
There's also the thematic closure — Wegg first appears at the dust-mounds, he profits from the dust-mounds, and he is ultimately returned to the dust. Or something very like it.
What I notice is the brief portrait of Wegg mid-air — his buttons on view, his wooden leg in a highly unaccommodating state.
Dickens has the cruelty of a very great cartoonist — he gives you the image you cannot forget, just before the humiliation is complete.
I feel slightly sorry for Wegg, even now. Which means it's working exactly as intended.
That is perhaps the surest sign of Dickens's genius — that even his comic villains retain the faintest claim on our sympathy, right up to the splash.
We've moved from the river to the rooftop to the rubbish cart — and in each case, Dickens has used the machinery of plot to tell us something precise about justice, memory, and what endures.
Our thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Oliver Trevelyan, and Caroline Woodcourt for this passage through the novel's hidden workings.
We'll be back shortly to take this further.

segments.title: Dickens's Voice: Narrative Technique and Social Truth

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the series where we take one of the great Victorian novels apart — carefully, lovingly — to see how it works.
Our Mutual Friend is Dickens at the height of his powers — and perhaps his darkest, most structurally ambitious book.
Each week we dig into a cluster of passages and ask: what is Dickens actually doing here, and why does it matter?
Today's segment is about Dickens's voice — the narrator as a force in the novel, and how that voice carries social truth.
Joining me are three brilliant readers of this novel.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who cares passionately about how fiction is built — the architecture of it, the craft decisions behind each effect.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has voiced more classic novels in audio than anyone alive — he hears this prose from the inside.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has never quite let it go.
Welcome, all three of you.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — and with one of the most unsettling small moments in the novel's opening.
Thank you — and what a place to start, because this passage from the opening chapter is, to my mind, one of the most quietly devastating pieces of prose Dickens ever wrote.
Gaffer Hexam has just pulled a body from the Thames — we understand that, though Dickens doesn't state it bluntly.
And then he finds money on the corpse, and here is what Dickens gives us.
'He chinked it once, and he blew upon it once, and he spat upon it once — for luck, he hoarsely said — before he put it in his pocket.'
Three verbs, each with 'once' attached — a liturgical rhythm, almost a ritual.
Dickens has turned the act of pocketing stolen money from the dead into something that looks disturbingly like prayer.
And the word 'hoarsely' — that's the stroke of genius.
It tells us everything: this man is not performing for anyone, this is simply what he does, and his voice is roughened by a life of it.
Eleanor's absolutely right about the rhythm — and when you read it aloud, which of course I have done, you feel it in your body before you understand it in your head.
Chink, blow, spit — it's almost percussive.
And the narrator doesn't flinch, doesn't editorialize, doesn't ask us to feel horrified.
The horror is already baked into the plainness of the telling.
And what I find fascinating is that Gaffer says 'for luck' — as if luck is what governs this transaction, not death, not robbery, not complicity.
He's domesticated the grotesque entirely.
What strikes me every time I return to this passage is the phrase 'the upper half of the man came back into the boat.'
'The upper half of the man' — not simply 'Gaffer' or 'he.'
Dickens is already fragmenting him, reducing him to parts, before we've even properly met him.
And he washes his arms — washes the money — but you can't wash the river off, can you.
The contamination runs the other way: it's Gaffer who is in the river's possession, not the other way around.
And that contamination, Caroline, carries forward all the way to Gaffer's own death — which Dickens delivers with almost grotesque irony.
When the body is finally recovered from the Thames, Riderhood — who has been pursuing Gaffer, who betrayed him — looks down and recognizes him.
And his response, those four words, is one of the bluntest sentences in the novel.
'Gaffer's done me. It's Gaffer!'
'Gaffer's done me' — even in death, the man is understood purely through what he costs other people.
The river has swallowed him, and Riderhood's only thought is that he's been cheated of something.
Dickens gives us no elegy, no softening — just that blunt, self-interested exclamation.
And that's the thing about Dickens's narrator in this novel — it never performs grief on behalf of characters who haven't earned it.
Gaffer lived by the river's logic, and the river applied it to him.
There's a terrible economy to it — the novel is full of terrible economies.
What I'd add is that 'It's Gaffer!' — that second exclamation — reads almost like recognition of a joke.
Not a funny joke. A cosmic one.
That phrase — cosmic joke — feels like exactly the right frame for what Caroline is going to bring us to next.
Because if the river passages show Dickens at his most gothic, the school passages show him at his most savage — and his most formally inventive.
Caroline, you've been sitting with that school scene — what's happening there?
The school passage is one of the moments in this novel where I simply stop and read it again, before I can move on.
Dickens describes a school — Charley Hexam's school — that is, to put it plainly, a catastrophe.
'Young women old in the vices of the commonest and worst life, were expected to profess themselves enthralled by the good child's book.'
There's a fury in 'old in the vices' — these are not innocent children being instructed, they are people the system is wilfully pretending are something they are not.
And the narrator's contempt is aimed squarely not at the pupils, but at the 'grimly ludicrous pretence' — the system's own self-flattery.
What's structurally brilliant about that passage is the way Dickens lets the prose itself enact the jumble it's describing.
He sets up a sentence about complexity and disorder, and then he does something I find almost dizzying.
'An exceedingly and confoundingly perplexing jumble of a school, in fact, where black spirits and grey, red spirits and white, jumbled jumbled jumbled jumbled, jumbled every night.'
That repeated 'jumbled' isn't just colour — it's a rhetorical enactment.
The sentence is doing to the reader exactly what the school does to its pupils: overwhelming, confusing, hammering the same meaningless syllable until it loses all content.
That is a very conscious craft decision, and it's audacious.
I have read that sentence aloud in at least two different recording studios and I will tell you — it is a gift and a trap simultaneously.
Because you have to get the four 'jumbleds' right — not too comic, not too flat — or the whole thing collapses.
But there's also the passage about the Sunday school — the 'chief executioner' and his acolyte smoothing children's faces.
Dickens calls the teacher a 'chief executioner' and the helper an 'executioner's assistant' — and that language is not hyperbole.
He means it. These children are being killed, quietly, in their imaginations.
And the image of the acolyte smoothing faces 'as if he were anointing them for a whisker' — it's both absurdly funny and genuinely appalling.
And then the children are 'exchanging measles, rashes, whooping-cough, fever, and stomach disorders, as if they were assembled in High Market for the purpose.'
The market image is devastating — Dickens is saying this is a transaction, a trade in disease and ignorance, dressed up as charity.
And what I keep coming back to is that this is Charley Hexam's school — Charley, who escapes the river, who wants so desperately to improve himself.
The novel is not sentimental about education as salvation. It sees the machinery behind the promise.
That tension — between aspiration and the systems that crush it — brings us to a very different kind of passage, and a very different emotional register.
Because the novel also has this remarkable capacity, just when you've been laughing or horrified, to go very quiet and very interior.
I want to bring everyone to the passage where Lizzie Hexam, after a conversation with Eugene Wrayburn, turns something over inside herself — and barely survives it.
This is one of my favourite moments in the entire novel, and I think it's one Dickens doesn't always get credit for.
Eugene has shown a moment of genuine earnestness — unusual for him — and it catches Lizzie entirely off guard.
And Dickens takes us right inside her, to this extraordinarily painful question she asks herself.

'She thought, had she, so far below him and so different, rejected this disinterestedness, because of some vain misgiving that he sought her out, or heeded any personal attractions that he might descry in her?'
She is ashamed of the very thought that he might find her attractive — she suspects herself of vanity, and it destroys her.
'Sinking before her own eyes' — that is such a precise phrase for a very specific kind of self-contempt.
What Dickens is doing technically in that passage is something quite remarkable — he's rendering the motion of consciousness, the way a feeling shifts shape as you examine it.
The narrator says Eugene's sudden earnestness sounded a 'subtle string' in Lizzie — and a string is exactly the right word.
It reverberates. It sets off harmonics she wasn't ready for.
And what I find extraordinary is the phrase 'inseparable from some touch of their opposites in her own breast.'
Dickens is saying that her recognition of goodness in Eugene activates an awareness of something — call it longing — in herself that she immediately reads as corruption.
It's psychologically complex in a way the novel is rarely given credit for.
I'd go further — I think it's one of the most honest depictions of what class does to the inner life of a person.
Lizzie doesn't think: I deserve this man's attention. She thinks: I must be imagining it, and my imagining it is shameful.
The class system has got all the way inside her, so deep she punishes herself for ordinary human feeling.
And the ending of it — she 'broke into silent tears' — is devastating precisely because it's silent.
No one sees this. No one knows. The narrator does, and we do, and that's the compact Dickens makes with his reader.
That compact — between narrator and reader, carried across every register from the gothic to the comic to the interior — is, I think, what we've been circling all through this conversation.
Dickens's voice in this novel is not a neutral instrument — it is a moral instrument, tuned very precisely.
Eleanor, Oliver, Caroline — thank you.
In the next segment, we'll be turning to money — the central obsession of this novel — and asking what Dickens thought he was doing when he made a fortune built on dust the engine of his plot.

segments.title: Closing: Transformation and Redemption in the River

utterances.text: We've spent this episode tracing the great currents of Our Mutual Friend — the river, the dust, the money, the mud.
For our closing segment, I want to sit with what the novel does to its characters — what it transforms, what it destroys, and what, against all odds, it redeems.
Because this is a novel full of people being made and unmade — sometimes by the river, sometimes by their own darker natures.
Eleanor, let's begin with destruction — specifically with Bradley Headstone, who seems to me one of Dickens's most frightening portraits of a man consumed from within.
Bradley Headstone is one of Dickens's genuinely terrifying achievements — and what makes him so is that the destruction is entirely internal.
There's a passage late in the novel that stopped me cold the first time I read it.

"Rigid before the fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more haggard, its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being overspread with ashes, and the very texture and colour of his hair degenerating."
That image of the charmed flame turning him old — it's sorcery used as psychological realism.
His body is literally enacting what obsession and guilt do to a person over years, compressed into a single night.
The ashes spreading across his face — Dickens is preparing us for a kind of living death before the actual one arrives.
When I read that passage aloud in the recording booth, I had to stop after the first take.
Not because I'd made an error — but because the rhythm of it does something almost physical to you.
The accumulation — deepening, haggard, whiter and whiter, degenerating — it's a sentence that refuses to stop its own decay.
And Riderhood is there, watching — which is its own particular horror.
This man whose false accusation set so much of the plot in motion, now silently witness to the ruin he helped create.
And speaking of Riderhood's false accusation — the brazenness of that opening accusation against Gaffer Hexam is extraordinary in its own right.
"His hand and no other" — Dickens gives him that terrible certainty, that rhetorical hammer-blow.
What strikes me about Riderhood is how Dickens lets him perform confidence he hasn't earned.
That whole scene of him turning the drowned cap over in his hands before he speaks — Dickens is staging a lie.
And then the declaration, so precisely worded — listen to it:
"The hand of Jesse Hexam, commonly called Gaffer on the river and along shore, is the hand that done that deed. His hand and no other."
That repetition of "hand" — it's almost incantatory.
And the brutality of it is that Gaffer can't answer — can't be cleared — because by the time the truth emerges, he's already dead.
The river takes him before justice can.
And that's so characteristic of this novel — justice is never clean, never arrives on time, never fully satisfies.
Which is why the moments of genuine happiness feel so hard-won — almost miraculous.
That little supper scene with Bella and John Rokesmith and her father — it's almost shocking in how tender it is, given everything the novel has put us through.
Dickens reaches for the fairy tale register — and it's completely earned.
The nursery hobgoblins are doing a lot of work in that passage.
Because the joke about the hobgoblins is precisely that the threat is absent — no thunderous growlings, no possessiveness, no discord.
Let me read the full comparison, because Dickens's phrasing is irresistible:

"It was, as Bella gaily said, like the supper provided for the three nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous low growlings of the alarming discovery, 'Somebody's been drinking my milk!'"
The word "gaily" — Bella says this gaily — that single adverb tells you everything about her transformation.
This is a woman who started the novel treating suitors like commodities on a market — now she's gaily comparing her supper to a children's story.
And there's something gloriously absurd about the iron safe of Chicksey, Veneering, and Stobbles lurking in the corner like a dull dragon.
"By far the most delicious that Bella, or John Rokesmith, or even R. Wilfer had ever made" — that "even" is doing something lovely.
R. Wilfer, dear bumbling R. Wilfer, has presumably eaten in more comfortable circumstances in his time.
But Dickens is saying: the quality of a meal has nothing to do with the food.
It has to do with who you're eating it with, and whether you've earned the right to sit at the table freely.
And Bella has, at last, genuinely earned it — not by being good, but by becoming herself.
That's the redemption this novel believes in — not moral correction imposed from outside, but an interior opening.
And set against Bradley Headstone's interior closing — that image of him whitening like ashes by the fire — the contrast couldn't be more stark.
One character opens into joy; the other calcifies into ruin.
And Dickens makes you feel both outcomes as entirely inevitable — which is the mark of a novelist who genuinely understands how people work.
That feels like the right place to leave it — and perhaps the most honest summary of what Our Mutual Friend achieves.
It holds the fairy-tale supper and the man turning to ashes in the same imaginative space — and makes both feel true.
My thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Oliver Trevelyan, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation that has been, in the best Dickensian spirit, delicious.
Our Mutual Friend Unpacked will return.

c9:p29.text:
These two ignorant and unpolished people had guided themselves so far on
      in their journey of life, by a religious sense of duty and desire to do
      right. Ten thousand weaknesses and absurdities might have been detected in
      the breasts of both; ten thousand vanities additional, possibly, in the
      breast of the woman. But the hard wrathful and sordid nature that had
      wrung as much work out of them as could be got in their best days, for as
      little money as could be paid to hurry on their worst, had never been so
      warped but that it knew their moral straightness and respected it. In its
      own despite, in a constant conflict with itself and them, it had done so.
      And this is the eternal law. For, Evil often stops short at itself and
      dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.
c9:p29.summary: Dickens reflects that the Boffins, though ignorant and unpolished, have been guided by genuine religious duty and moral righteousness that even hardened souls cannot entirely resist.
c9:p29.best_quote: For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.

c64:p101.text:
‘Now, scoundrel,’ he pursued, ‘I am going to finish. You supposed me just
      now, to be the possessor of my father’s property.—So I am. But
      through any act of my father’s, or by any right I have? No. Through the
      munificence of Mr Boffin. The conditions that he made with me, before
      parting with the secret of the Dutch bottle, were, that I should take the
      fortune, and that he should take his Mound and no more. I owe everything I
      possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness,
      goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin. And
      when, knowing what I knew, I saw such a mud-worm as you presume to rise in
      this house against this noble soul, the wonder is,’ added John Harmon
      through his clenched teeth, and with a very ugly turn indeed on Wegg’s
      cravat, ‘that I didn’t try to twist your head off, and fling  that  out of
      window! So. That’s the last short speech, do you understand?’
c64:p101.summary: Harmon explains that he owes his fortune entirely to Boffin's generosity, and his fury at Wegg's presumption against such a noble soul.
c64:p101.best_quote: I owe everything I possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness, goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin.

c67:p57.text:
When I devised this story, I foresaw the likelihood that a class of
      readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to
      conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John
      Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he. Pleasing myself
      with the idea that the supposition might in part arise out of some
      ingenuity in the story, and thinking it worth while, in the interests of
      art, to hint to an audience that an artist (of whatever denomination) may
      perhaps be trusted to know what he is about in his vocation, if they will
      concede him a little patience, I was not alarmed by the anticipation.
c67:p57.summary: Dickens explains that he intentionally created ambiguity about John Harmon's identity and asks readers to trust his artistic judgment and patience with the serialized format.
c67:p57.best_quote: I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he.

c18:p149.text:
‘The child’s father is employed by the house that employs me; that’s how I
      came to know it, Charley. The father is like his own father, a weak
      wretched trembling creature, falling to pieces, never sober. But a good
      workman too, at the work he does. The mother is dead. This poor ailing
      little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people
      from her cradle—if she ever had one, Charley.’
c18:p149.summary: Lizzie explains that Bella's father is employed by her employer and shares his father's weakness for drink; her mother is dead, and the child is surrounded by alcoholics and degradation.
c18:p149.best_quote: This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle—if she ever had one, Charley.

c30:p7.text:
‘When I came to England, attracted to the country with which I had none
      but most miserable associations, by the accounts of my fine inheritance
      that found me abroad, I came back, shrinking from my father’s money,
      shrinking from my father’s memory, mistrustful of being forced on a
      mercenary wife, mistrustful of my father’s intention in thrusting that
      marriage on me, mistrustful that I was already growing avaricious,
      mistrustful that I was slackening in gratitude to the two dear noble
      honest friends who had made the only sunlight in my childish life or that
      of my heartbroken sister. I came back, timid, divided in my mind, afraid
      of myself and everybody here, knowing of nothing but wretchedness that my
      father’s wealth had ever brought about. Now, stop, and so far think it
      out, John Harmon. Is that so? That is exactly so.
c30:p7.summary: John Harmon explains that he returned to England reluctantly, conflicted about his inherited wealth, fearful of a mercenary marriage, and anxious about his own character.
c30:p7.best_quote: I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife

c30:p9.text:
‘However, a sociable word or two on these mistakes became an easy
      introduction between us, and the weather was hot, and he helped me to a
      cool cabin on deck alongside his own, and his first school had been at
      Brussels as mine had been, and he had learnt French as I had learnt it,
      and he had a little history of himself to relate—God only knows how
      much of it true, and how much of it false—that had its likeness to
      mine. I had been a seaman too. So we got to be confidential together, and
      the more easily yet, because he and every one on board had known by
      general rumour what I was making the voyage to England for. By such
      degrees and means, he came to the knowledge of my uneasiness of mind, and
      of its setting at that time in the direction of desiring to see and form
      some judgment of my allotted wife, before she could possibly know me for
      myself; also to try Mrs Boffin and give her a glad surprise. So the plot
      was made out of our getting common sailors’ dresses (as he was able to
      guide me about London), and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer’s
      neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way, and doing whatever
      chance might favour on the spot, and seeing what came of it. If nothing
      came of it, I should be no worse off, and there would merely be a short
      delay in my presenting myself to Lightwood. I have all these facts right?
      Yes. They are all accurately right.
c30:p9.summary: John Harmon describes the scheme he and Radfoot devised to dress as common sailors, observe Bella Wilfer, surprise Mrs Boffin, and determine the authenticity of Bella's character before revealing himself to Lightwood.
c30:p9.best_quote: the plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses (as he was able to guide me about London), and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way

c31:p1.text:
He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the
      latter.
c31:p1.summary: Rokesmith justifies his original deception as harmless, traces how it spiralled beyond his control, and wrestles with the impossible choice between disgracing Bella or deceiving the Boffins.

c31:p109.text:
‘I don’t. And if  they  do, my dear, they ought to learn better,’ said Mr
      Boffin. ‘Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses,
      and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and
      Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities
      that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among ’em pretty well up to
      his neck! If Mr Tom Noakes gives his five shillings ain’t he a Patron, and
      if Mrs Jack Styles gives her five shillings ain’t she a Patroness? What
      the deuce is it all about? If it ain’t stark staring impudence, what do
      you call it?’
c31:p109.summary: Mr Boffin delivers a scathing critique of the proliferation of patronage titles and the pretension of charity donors who expect public recognition for their contributions.

c2:p2.text:
There was an innocent piece of dinner-furniture that went upon easy
      castors and was kept over a livery stable-yard in Duke Street, Saint
      James’s, when not in use, to whom the Veneerings were a source of blind
      confusion. The name of this article was Twemlow. Being first cousin to
      Lord Snigsworth, he was in frequent requisition, and at many houses might
      be said to represent the dining-table in its normal state. Mr and Mrs
      Veneering, for example, arranging a dinner, habitually started with
      Twemlow, and then put leaves in him, or added guests to him. Sometimes,
      the table consisted of Twemlow and half a dozen leaves; sometimes, of
      Twemlow and a dozen leaves; sometimes, Twemlow was pulled out to his
      utmost extent of twenty leaves. Mr and Mrs Veneering on occasions of
      ceremony faced each other in the centre of the board, and thus the
      parallel still held; for, it always happened that the more Twemlow was
      pulled out, the further he found himself from the center, and nearer to
      the sideboard at one end of the room, or the window-curtains at the other.
c2:p2.summary: Twemlow, a man of good family connections, is introduced through an extended metaphor comparing him to a dining table that the Veneerings manipulate for social purposes.

c27:p51.text:
The consideration of Mrs Boffin had clothed Mr Sloppy in a suit of black,
      on which the tailor had received personal directions from Rokesmith to
      expend the utmost cunning of his art, with a view to the concealment of
      the cohering and sustaining buttons. But, so much more powerful were the
      frailties of Sloppy’s form than the strongest resources of tailoring
      science, that he now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way
      of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a
      hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators. The
      artistic taste of some unknown hatter had furnished him with a hatband of
      wholesale capacity which was fluted behind, from the crown of his hat to
      the brim, and terminated in a black bunch, from which the imagination
      shrunk discomfited and the reason revolted. Some special powers with which
      his legs were endowed, had already hitched up his glossy trousers at the
      ankles, and bagged them at the knees; while similar gifts in his arms had
      raised his coat-sleeves from his wrists and accumulated them at his
      elbows. Thus set forth, with the additional embellishments of a very
      little tail to his coat, and a yawning gulf at his waistband, Sloppy stood
      confessed.
c27:p51.summary: Sloppy's new black suit is a comedic disaster: buttons gleam like eyes, the hatband is absurdly fluted, his sleeves ride up and trousers bag at the knees, and his coat has a yawning gap at the waistband.
c27:p51.best_quote: he now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators.

c64:p67.text:
Somebody else had come in quietly by the folding-doors. Turning his head,
      Wegg beheld his persecutor, the ever-wakeful dustman, accoutred with
      fantail hat and velveteen smalls complete. Who, untying his tied-up broken
      head, revealed a head that was whole, and a face that was Sloppy’s.

c40:p72.text:
On this head, Silas Wegg had much to say. Silas had to say That, he would
      beg to remind his comrade, brother, and partner, of the impressive
      passages they had read that evening; of the evident parallel in Mr
      Boffin’s mind between them and the late owner of the Bower, and the
      present circumstances of the Bower; of the bottle; and of the box. That,
      the fortunes of his brother and comrade, and of himself were evidently
      made, inasmuch as they had but to put their price upon this document, and
      get that price from the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour: who
      now appeared to be less of a minion and more of a worm than had been
      previously supposed. That, he considered it plain that such price was
      stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, ‘Halves!’
      That, the question then arose when ‘Halves!’ should be called. That, here
      he had a plan of action to recommend, with a conditional clause. That, the
      plan of action was that they should lie by with patience; that, they
      should allow the Mounds to be gradually levelled and cleared away, while
      retaining to themselves their present opportunity of watching the process—which
      would be, he conceived, to put the trouble and cost of daily digging and
      delving upon somebody else, while they might nightly turn such complete
      disturbance of the dust to the account of their own private investigations—and
      that, when the Mounds were gone, and they had worked those chances for
      their own joint benefit solely, they should then, and not before, explode
      on the minion and worm. But here came the conditional clause, and to this
      he entreated the special attention of his comrade, brother, and partner.
      It was not to be borne that the minion and worm should carry off any of
      that property which was now to be regarded as their own property. When he,
      Mr Wegg, had seen the minion surreptitiously making off with that bottle,
      and its precious contents unknown, he had looked upon him in the light of
      a mere robber, and, as such, would have despoiled him of his ill-gotten
      gain, but for the judicious interference of his comrade, brother, and
      partner. Therefore, the conditional clause he proposed was, that, if the
      minion should return in his late sneaking manner, and if, being closely
      watched, he should be found to possess himself of anything, no matter
      what, the sharp sword impending over his head should be instantly shown
      him, he should be strictly examined as to what he knew or suspected,
      should be severely handled by them his masters, and should be kept in a
      state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should
      see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his
      possessions. If, said Mr Wegg by way of peroration, he had erred in saying
      only ‘Halves!’ he trusted to his comrade, brother, and partner not to
      hesitate to set him right, and to reprove his weakness. It might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Two-thirds; it might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Three-fourths. On those points
      he was ever open to correction.
c40:p72.summary: Wegg proposes an elaborate scheme: let Boffin excavate the Mounds at his own expense while they observe, then when the work is done, threaten him with the earlier will and extort half his property. If Boffin is caught secretly removing anything, they will interrogate and enslave him morally until he pays for his freedom.

c49:p45.text:
Sooth to say, Mr Rokesmith not only passed the window, but came into the
      counting-house. And not only came into the counting-house, but, finding
      himself alone there with Bella and her father, rushed at Bella and caught
      her in his arms, with the rapturous words ‘My dear, dear girl; my gallant,
      generous, disinterested, courageous, noble girl!’ And not only that even,
      (which one might have thought astonishment enough for one dose), but
      Bella, after hanging her head for a moment, lifted it up and laid it on
      his breast, as if that were her head’s chosen and lasting resting-place!
c49:p45.summary: John Rokesmith bursts into the counting-house and declares his passionate love for Bella, who reciprocates by resting her head on his breast in acceptance.

And not only that even, (which one might have thought astonishment enough for one dose), but Bella, after hanging her head for a moment, lifted it up and laid it on his breast, as if that were her head's chosen and lasting resting-place!

c8:p43.text:
‘The last time me and Mrs Boffin saw the poor boy,’ said Mr Boffin,
      warming (as fat usually does) with a tendency to melt, ‘he was a child of
      seven year old. For when he came back to make intercession for his sister,
      me and Mrs Boffin were away overlooking a country contract which was to be
      sifted before carted, and he was come and gone in a single hour. I say he
      was a child of seven year old. He was going away, all alone and forlorn,
      to that foreign school, and he come into our place, situate up the yard of
      the present Bower, to have a warm at our fire. There was his little scanty
      travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in
      the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the
      steamboat, as the old man wouldn’t hear of allowing a sixpence
      coach-money. Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a
      full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two
      open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks; but seeing the tears come
      into the child’s eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him
      round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, “I’d
      give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!” I don’t say but
      what it cut me, and but what it at the same time heightened my feelings of
      admiration for Mrs Boffin. The poor child clings to her for awhile, as she
      clings to him, and then, when the old man calls, he says “I must go! God
      bless you!” and for a moment rests his heart against her bosom, and looks
      up at both of us, as if it was in pain—in agony. Such a look! I went
      aboard with him (I gave him first what little treat I thought he’d like),
      and I left him when he had fallen asleep in his berth, and I came back to
      Mrs Boffin. But tell her what I would of how I had left him, it all went
      for nothing, for, according to her thoughts, he never changed that look
      that he had looked up at us two. But it did one piece of good. Mrs Boffin
      and me had no child of our own, and had sometimes wished that how we had
      one. But not now. “We might both of us die,” says Mrs Boffin, “and other
      eyes might see that lonely look in our child.” So of a night, when it was
      very cold, or when the wind roared, or the rain dripped heavy, she would
      wake sobbing, and call out in a fluster, “Don’t you see the poor child’s
      face? O shelter the poor child!”—till in course of years it gently
      wore out, as many things do.’
c8:p43.summary: Boffin recounts the last time he and Mrs Boffin saw young John Harmon, a seven-year-old being sent to a foreign school, including the poignant moment when Mrs Boffin wept while warming the boy by the fire and embraced him protectively, expressing a desire to save him—a memory that haunted her for years.
